newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian meeting fails on black deaths reduction.
newsitem.headline: Australian meeting fails on black deaths reduction.

text.p: An historic meeting of Australian government leaders and Aboriginal officials on Friday broke up without settling on a united strategy to combat the unusually high number of Aborigines dying in jails and police cells.
The first top level meeting of key indigenous leaders and national and state ministers in charge of native issues could not agree on how to cut the number of black deaths in custody.
But the national government's Aboriginal Affairs Minister, John Herron, insisted at least some progress had been made.
"It is a start, we have got to work from here. We don't believe this is the be-all and end-all by any manner of means," Herron told reporters.

Native Australians represent less than two percent of the nation's 18 million people but account for more than 25 percent of deaths in official custody, despite a half-decade campaign to combat such deaths.
They are also 17 times more likely than whites to be jailed, often on minor charges such as public drunkenness.
The meeting agreed on an ill-defined, general plan to reduce Aboriginal deaths in custody but Australia's native human rights chief and some other Aboriginal groups refused to sign on.

"Quite frankly, the document that has been signed off merely commits the states and the territories to go away and have a look at what they might do," Aboriginal delegate and dissident Michael Mansell told reporters.
Human Rights and Equal Opportunity Commission indigenous social justice commissioner Mick Dodson also refused to sign any settlement.

The national and state governments, except the Northern Territory -- the administration with the highest proportion of Aboriginal voters -- agreed in their pact to address broad social, economic, cultural, justice, customary law and law reform issues, without going into details.
But the meeting failed to set specific strategies to reduce the number of native Aborigines and Torres Strait Islanders dying in custody and arrests.
"Regrettably, this communique has left the opportunity for more foot-dragging and further excuses," said Labor opposition acting Aboriginal Affairs spokesman Duncan Kerr.

Despite a long and detailed national inquiry in the early 1990s, the number of Aborigines dying in Australia's jails and police cells continues to grow as state governments fail to fully implement steps to curb such deaths.
Aboriginal deaths in custody jumped 49 percent to 19 in the year to June 30, 1996 -- the most deaths since official figures began in 1990/91 -- the latest official figures show.
The increase comes as total deaths in custody are falling.
